newsitem.title: NORWAY: Storebrand holders rejection of merge no surprise.
newsitem.headline: Storebrand holders rejection of merge no surprise.

text.p: The rejection by shareholders in Norway's largest insurance group Storebrand ASA of a proposal to merge with Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse ASA was not a major surprise despite the fact that Storebrand's board had recommended the move, analysts said.
Analysts said the outcome came as little surprise following much jostling among Storebrand shareholders since the proposal was announced at the beginning the April.

Many had expressed concern over the state's ownership in the planned financial giant. The state holds more than 50 percent of Christiania Bank after the government rescued it along with several other banks from a financial crisis between 1988 and 1992. This would have translated to a 25 pecent stake in Christiania Group.

"It's been on the cards for a while," James Alexander, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London, told Reuters. "Norwegian industry -- the main opposition (to the merger) -- has said it does not want to do business with a company which has a large state ownership."

Most of the speculation building up to the Storebrand vote centred on two major shareholders, Norwegian conglomerate Orkla ASA and billionaire entrepreneur Kjell Inge Roekke. Both hold around 10 percent in Storebrand.
Orkla announced to shareholders before the ballot that it would go against the deal.
"Our summary is that there are opportunities with the merger, but here is also uncertainty. We will vote no," Tom Vidar Rygh, Orkla head of investment, told the meeting.
Roekke declined to comment on his decision, but the mathematics of the vote indicated a no.
Storebrand's two other major shareholders, Norwegian state pension fund, Folketrygdfondet, and U.S. hedge fund, Tiger Management Corp, previously indicated that they would support the plans.

Shareholders in Christiania Bank, Norway's second largest bank, had agreed to the plan, approving the merger by 389,947,000 shares, or 99.86 percent of the equity represented at its extraordinary meeting, with 556,900 shares against.
In a statement, Christiania Bank chairman, Harald Arnkvaern, said the bank would continue to work towards the same strategic objectives as before the Storebrand shareholders' decision.

"Although it is difficult to find an alternative which will truely equal a merger with Storebrand, the merger process has entailed a number of very useful strategic clarifications where Christiania Bank is concerned, both with regard to the Norwegian state's participation as owner and possible structural changes in the financial markets in future," Arnkvaern said.

A two-thirds majority of Storebrand shareholders voting "Yes" was required to push through the fusion to form Christiania Group, which would have been the country's largest financial institution and the sixth biggest in the Nordic region.

The vote remained on a knife edge to the very end and supporters of the plan managed to drum up only 62.07 percent of the votes, or 171,062,281 shares, represented at the extraordinary general meeting.

"We who believed that the merger proposal was strategically right, we are sorry about the result," Jon Gundersen, Storebrand's chairman, said. "At the same time we accept that the shareholders have spoken."
